docs.text:
Troy Reynolds Datasheet as part of Fill-A-Bot for Team 201

Individual Subsystem: Liquid Amount Sensing

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
This datasheet documents the design and development of my individual Liquid Amount Sensing subsystem for the Fill-A-Bot project. The subsystem is responsible for measuring the amount of liquid in the system and providing this information to the rest of the embedded system.

The subsystem uses a load cell to measure weight. Because a load cell produces a very small differential voltage, a load-cell ADC/amplifier is used to amplify and digitize the signal before it is processed by the PIC18F57Q43 microcontroller.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text:
The Fill-A-Bot is a team embedded-systems project consisting of multiple subsystems that work together to control and monitor the movement and dispensing of liquid.

My portion of the project is the Liquid Amount Sensing subsystem. Its purpose is to measure the amount of liquid present so that the system can monitor changes in liquid quantity and provide measurement data to the main controller.

The subsystem is based around a load cell, load-cell ADC/amplifier, and PIC18F57Q43 microcontroller.

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text:
My individual contribution is the design and implementation of the Liquid Amount Sensing subsystem. This includes selecting the sensing components, designing the electrical connections, interfacing the sensor electronics with the PIC18F57Q43, and documenting the subsystem.

The major components selected for the subsystem are a Soldered Electronics 555026 1 kg load cell and a SparkFun SEN-13879 HX711 load-cell ADC/amplifier.

The following sections document the development of my subsystem:

  • Block Diagram
  • Component Selection
  • Bill of Materials
  • Schematic
  • Power Budget

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The individual block diagram documents the electrical design of the Liquid Amount Sensing subsystem for Fill-A-Bot. The subsystem measures the amount of liquid using a 1 kg load cell connected to a Nuvoton NAU7802 24-bit load-cell ADC. A PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano reads the NAU7802 using I2C and communicates with the Fill-A-Bot system using UART.

The subsystem includes its own 5 V power regulation, load-cell interface, ADC circuitry, team communication interface, GPIO expansion, debugging circuitry, and test points.

docs.title: Individual Block Diagram
docs.text: Figure 1: Individual block diagram for the Fill-A-Bot Liquid Amount Sensing subsystem.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
The subsystem accepts a 9–12 V DC input through a 2-position screw-terminal connector. The input passes through a 500 mA fuse before reaching an LM7805CT linear voltage regulator.

The LM7805CT converts the input voltage to a regulated 5 V supply for the subsystem. A 0.33 µF capacitor is connected at the regulator input and a 0.1 µF capacitor is connected at the regulator output.

A local 5 V selection jumper is included between the locally regulated supply and the +5V_BOARD rail.

docs.title: Liquid Amount Sensing
docs.text:
A 1 kg Soldered Electronics 555026 load cell is used to measure the weight of the liquid. The load cell connects to the sensor board through four connections: A+, A−, E+, and E−.

The differential output from the load cell is connected to a Nuvoton NAU7802 24-bit load-cell ADC. The analog input includes two 47 Ω resistors and filtering to condition the low-level differential signal before conversion.

The NAU7802 communicates with the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano using I2C. SDA and SCL use 4.7 kΩ pull-up resistors. The NAU7802 DRDY signal is also connected to the Curiosity Nano to indicate when a new ADC conversion is available.

docs.title: Team Communication
docs.text:
The Liquid Amount Sensing subsystem communicates with the Fill-A-Bot system using UART through the 8-pin team connector.

The team UART transmit signal is connected to the UART receive input of the Curiosity Nano, and the Curiosity Nano UART transmit output is connected to the team UART receive signal.

The connector also provides a common ground connection. Unused connector positions are left unconnected.

docs.title: GPIO Expansion
docs.text: A 6-pin expansion header provides four general-purpose I/O signals labeled GPIO1 through GPIO4. The header also provides +5V_BOARD and GND for connection to additional external hardware.

docs.title: Debugging and Test Points
docs.text:
A green debug LED is connected to the Curiosity Nano through a 1.2 kΩ current-limiting resistor.

A momentary debug pushbutton is provided with a 10 kΩ pull-up resistor and a 1 µF capacitor for hardware debounce.

Five test points are included for important power, ground, and ADC-related signals to support debugging and subsystem verification.

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text:
Individual Subsystem: Liquid Amount Sensing

The Liquid Amount Sensing subsystem measures the amount of liquid in the Fill-A-Bot using a load cell. The small differential signal from the load cell must be amplified and converted into digital data before it can be processed by the PIC18F57Q43 microcontroller. The following sections compare potential load cells and load-cell ADC/amplifier solutions for this subsystem.

docs.title: Load Cell Selection
docs.text:
Table 1: Load cell component selection

Load Cell / Weight Sensor

Solution Pros Cons Option 1Soldered Electronics 5550261 kg Load Cell$15.96/eachLink to product * 1 kg maximum load is appropriate for the liquid container* Operates from 5 V to 10 V* 2 ±0.1 mV/V output sensitivity* Wheatstone bridge design works with a load-cell ADC* Manufacturer specifically recommends an HX711 interface * More expensive than the Adafruit option* Requires an ADC/amplifier to measure the small output signal* Requires calibration* DigiKey currently lists the part as out of stock Option 2Adafruit Industries 45401 kgf Load Cell$3.95/eachLink to product * 1 kg measurement range is appropriate for the project* Lowest-cost load cell of the three options* Compact load-cell design* Large quantity available from DigiKey * Requires an external ADC/amplifier* Requires calibration before accurate measurements can be made* Available documentation provides less electrical information than the Soldered load cell Option 3Seeed Technology 3149900000-500 g Load Cell$17.00/eachLink to product * Designed for electronic weighing applications* Recommended 5 V excitation matches the subsystem supply* 0.5 ±0.1 mV/V output sensitivity* ±0.05% full-scale nonlinearity specification * Maximum capacity is only 500 g* Container plus liquid could exceed the 500 g limit* Most expensive load-cell option* Requires an external ADC/amplifier

Choice: Option 1: Soldered Electronics 555026 1 kg Load Cell

Rationale: The Soldered Electronics 555026 was selected because its 1 kg maximum load provides an appropriate measurement range for the liquid container used in the Fill-A-Bot. The sensor operates from a 5 V to 10 V excitation supply and produces a 2 ±0.1 mV/V output from its Wheatstone bridge. This allows it to operate from the subsystem's 5 V supply and interface with a high-resolution load-cell ADC. The manufacturer's documentation also specifically recommends using an HX711 to amplify and digitize the small load-cell output. Although this option is more expensive than the Adafruit load cell, its documented electrical characteristics and compatibility with the selected ADC provide greater confidence in the final design.

docs.title: Load Cell ADC / Amplifier Selection
docs.text:
Table 2: Load cell ADC/amplifier component selection

Load Cell ADC / Amplifier

Solution Pros Cons Option 1SparkFun Electronics SEN-13879HX711 Load Cell Amplifier$11.50/eachLink to product * 24-bit ADC designed specifically for weigh scales and bridge sensors* Built-in low-noise programmable gain amplifier* Selectable gain of 32, 64, or 128* Operates from 2.6 V to 5.5 V* Complete breakout board simplifies prototyping* Simple clock and data interface to the microcontroller * More expensive than a bare ADC IC* Maximum standard sample rate is 80 SPS* Does not use the standard I2C protocol* Requires software calibration for accurate weight measurements Option 2Nuvoton Technology NAU7802KGI24-bit Load Cell ADC$2.26/eachLink to product * 24-bit sigma-delta ADC designed for bridge and strain-gauge sensors* Programmable gain from 1 to 128* I2C-compatible interface* Operates from 2.7 V to 5.5 V* Through-hole 16-PDIP package is convenient for prototyping* Significantly less expensive than the HX711 module * Bare IC requires additional support circuitry* More software configuration is required* Requires register configuration over I2C* More complex to integrate than a complete breakout board Option 3Texas Instruments ADS1232IPWR24-bit Bridge Sensor ADC$8.50/eachLink to product * 24-bit ADC specifically designed for bridge sensors and weigh scales* Low-noise programmable gain amplifier* Selectable gains of 1, 2, 64, and 128* Two differential input channels* Operates from 2.7 V to 5.3 V* 10 SPS mode provides strong 50 Hz and 60 Hz noise rejection * Surface-mount 24-TSSOP package is more difficult to prototype* Requires additional external support components* More complex PCB layout than the HX711 breakout board* More expensive than the NAU7802 bare IC

Choice: Option 1: SparkFun Electronics SEN-13879 HX711 Load Cell Amplifier

Rationale: The SparkFun SEN-13879 HX711 was selected because the HX711 is specifically designed to interface directly with Wheatstone-bridge load cells. It combines a 24-bit ADC with a low-noise programmable gain amplifier, allowing the very small differential output from the selected load cell to be measured without a separate external amplifier. The device operates from 2.6 V to 5.5 V, making it compatible with the subsystem's 5 V supply. The SparkFun board also contains the supporting circuitry needed for the HX711, which simplifies prototyping and reduces PCB design risk. Although the NAU7802 is less expensive and provides an I2C-compatible interface, the complete HX711 breakout board provides the simplest implementation for the Liquid Amount Sensing subsystem.

This Component Selection page is still partly the old HX711 design, so we need to update it to match the final schematic.

The Load Cell Selection section is mostly good. The ADC selection, rationale, and pin table are what really need changing.

  1. Load Cell Selection Keep the three-option comparison and keep:

Choice: Option 1 — Soldered Electronics 555026 / 100382

But change the end of your rationale. Right now it says the manufacturer recommends the HX711 and then implies compatibility with your selected ADC. Since you're actually using the NAU7802, I'd use this finished version:

Choice: Option 1: Soldered Electronics 555026 1 kg Load Cell

Rationale: The Soldered Electronics 555026 was selected because its 1 kg maximum load provides an appropriate measurement range for the liquid container used in the Fill-A-Bot. The sensor operates from a 5 V to 10 V excitation supply and produces a 2 ±0.1 mV/V differential output from its Wheatstone bridge. This allows the load cell to operate from the subsystem's regulated 5 V supply and interface with a high-resolution bridge-sensor ADC. Although this option is more expensive than the Adafruit load cell, its documented electrical characteristics, 1 kg measurement range, and compatibility with the selected NAU7802 load-cell ADC make it well suited for the Liquid Amount Sensing subsystem.

The load-cell datasheet supports the 1 kg capacity, 5–10 V excitation and 2 ±0.1 mV/V output.

  1. ADC selection — this is the big change Your comparison table can stay. Having the HX711, NAU7802 and ADS1232 as the three candidates is good.

But change:

Choice: Option 1: SparkFun SEN-13879 HX711

to:

Choice: Option 2: Nuvoton Technology NAU7802KGI

Then replace the HX711 rationale with:

Choice: Option 2: Nuvoton Technology NAU7802KGI

Rationale: The Nuvoton Technology NAU7802KGI was selected because it combines a 24-bit sigma-delta ADC with a programmable gain amplifier designed for precision bridge and strain-gauge measurements. Its programmable gain allows the very small differential output of the load cell to be amplified before analog-to-digital conversion. The device operates from 2.7 V to 5.5 V, making it compatible with the subsystem's regulated 5 V supply. The NAU7802KGI is also available in a 16-PDIP through-hole package, allowing the ADC to be integrated directly onto the subsystem PCB without using a separate daughter board. At approximately $2.26 per device, it is also significantly less expensive than the HX711 breakout board and ADS1232 option. These characteristics make the NAU7802KGI the best fit for the final Liquid Amount Sensing subsystem.

  1. Update the NAU7802 pros/cons slightly Your Option 2 row is already pretty good. I'd keep most of it.

One wording change:

I2C-compatible interface

can stay here because this is describing the NAU7802 IC itself, not your team-board communication.

Also keep:

Bare IC requires additional support circuitry

because your final schematic actually demonstrates that—you added the filter capacitors, resistors, pull-ups, etc.

  1. The entire Pin Table needs replacing The existing table is still entirely HX711-based.

Delete it and use your final hardware connections instead:

Component Pin / Signal Connection Purpose Soldered 555026 Load Cell E+ / Input+ +5V_BOARD Positive bridge excitation Soldered 555026 Load Cell E− / Input− GND Negative bridge excitation Soldered 555026 Load Cell A+ / Output+ R2 → NAU7802 VIN1P Positive differential measurement Soldered 555026 Load Cell A− / Output− R1 → NAU7802 VIN1N Negative differential measurement NAU7802KGI VIN1P Load cell A+ through 47 Ω Positive ADC differential input NAU7802KGI VIN1N Load cell A− through 47 Ω Negative ADC differential input NAU7802KGI SDIO PIC RB2 ADC digital data NAU7802KGI SCLK PIC RB1 ADC digital clock NAU7802KGI DRDY PIC RC0 Indicates new ADC conversion is ready PIC18F57Q43 RA3 J1 Pin 1 — TEAM_IN Direct digital input from team controller PIC18F57Q43 RA4 J1 Pin 2 — TEAM_OUT Direct digital output to team controller PIC18F57Q43 RA0 SW1 TARE/ZERO Tare/zero button input PIC18F57Q43 RC1 R3 → LED1 Status LED output J1 Pin 1 TEAM_IN Team direct digital input J1 Pin 2 TEAM_OUT Team direct digital output J1 Pins 3–7 NC Unused J1 Pin 8 GND Common team ground That also makes your documentation consistent with the block diagram we just rebuilt.

So don't rewrite the whole page You only need to make three meaningful changes:

Load-cell rationale: remove the HX711-centered ending.

ADC choice: change Option 1 HX711 → Option 2 NAU7802KGI and replace its rationale.

Pin table: replace the HX711 table with the final NAU7802/PIC/team connections.

Do those and your Component Selection page will finally match the current PCB design.

Solution Pros Cons Option 1SparkFun Electronics SEN-13879HX711 Load Cell Amplifier$11.50/eachLink to product * 24-bit ADC designed specifically for weigh scales and bridge sensors* Built-in low-noise programmable gain amplifier* Selectable gain of 32, 64, or 128* Operates from 2.6 V to 5.5 V* Complete breakout board simplifies prototyping* Simple clock and data interface to the microcontroller * More expensive than a bare ADC IC* Maximum standard sample rate is 80 SPS* Breakout-board implementation is not appropriate for direct integration into the final subsystem PCB* Requires software calibration for accurate weight measurements Option 2Nuvoton Technology NAU7802KGI24-bit Load Cell ADC$2.26/eachLink to product * 24-bit sigma-delta ADC designed for bridge and strain-gauge sensors* Programmable gain from 1 to 128* Digital SDIO/SCLK interface to the microcontroller* Operates from 2.7 V to 5.5 V* Through-hole 16-PDIP package is convenient for PCB integration* Significantly less expensive than the HX711 module * Bare IC requires additional support circuitry* More software configuration is required* Requires configuration before measurements can be taken* More complex to integrate than a complete breakout board Option 3Texas Instruments ADS1232IPWR24-bit Bridge Sensor ADC$8.50/eachLink to product * 24-bit ADC specifically designed for bridge sensors and weigh scales* Low-noise programmable gain amplifier* Selectable gains of 1, 2, 64, and 128* Two differential input channels* Operates from 2.7 V to 5.3 V* 10 SPS mode provides strong 50 Hz and 60 Hz noise rejection * Surface-mount 24-TSSOP package is more difficult to prototype* Requires additional external support components* More complex PCB layout than the other options* More expensive than the NAU7802 bare IC

Choice: Option 2: Nuvoton Technology NAU7802KGI

Rationale: The Nuvoton Technology NAU7802KGI was selected because it combines a 24-bit sigma-delta ADC with a programmable gain amplifier designed for precision bridge and strain-gauge measurements. Its programmable gain allows the very small differential output of the load cell to be amplified before analog-to-digital conversion. The device operates from 2.7 V to 5.5 V, making it compatible with the subsystem's regulated 5 V supply. The NAU7802KGI is also available in a 16-PDIP through-hole package, allowing the ADC to be integrated directly onto the subsystem PCB without using a separate daughter board. At approximately $2.26 per device, it is also significantly less expensive than the HX711 breakout board and ADS1232 option. These characteristics make the NAU7802KGI the best fit for the final Liquid Amount Sensing subsystem.
